newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Senior U.S. official meets Taiwan's president.
newsitem.headline: Senior U.S. official meets Taiwan's president.

text.p: U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers met Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui on Tuesday, officials said, in the most senior U.S.-Taiwan contact in nearly two years and one certain to anger China.
"President Lee met with Deputy Secretary Summers at 9.30 a.m., and the meeting ended at 10.30 a.m.," a presidential spokeswoman told Reuters by telephone.
Details of the meeting were not immediately available.
It was the most senior U.S.-Taiwan contact since a visit to the Nationalist-ruled island by U.S. Transportation Secretary Federico Pena in December 1994.

The Lee-Summers talks came more than a year after Lee's politically explosive visit to the United States in June 1995, an ostensibly private trip that included no known meetings with U.S. officials but nonetheless outraged China.
China, Taiwan's arch rival since a civil war split them in 1949, regards Taiwan as a rebel province not entitled to sovereign contacts with foreign governments.
Beijing indicated last week that it would be unhappy if Summers visited Taiwan and held meetings with senior officials.
Summers on Monday acknowledged discussing trade and other bilateral issues in meetings with economics Vice-Minister Hsu Ke-sheng and other financial and foreign affairs officials.

Summers, at a news conference after those meetings, declined to comment on the political sensitivities surrounding his visit, but said such meetings would continue into the "indefinite future" as a matter of U.S. policy.

China exploded in protest after President Lee's high-profile U.S. visit, saying it showed that Taiwan wanted independence rather than reunification with the mainland, and that Washington was colluding in the scheme.

Beijing responded by downgrading its U.S. ties, suspending semi-official talks with Taipei and launching nearly nine months of war games and missile tests in waters near Taiwan in what it said was intended to thwart Taiwan's independence bid.
China has threatened to retake Taiwan by force if it opts for independence.
